strengths: The paper identifies an interesting limitation of standard unlearning metrics: even when a model misclassifies forget data, the true label can still remain in a conformal prediction set, as shown by their in-set ratio diagnostics (Table 3).

It proposes two new evaluation metrics, CR and MIACR, motivated by conformal prediction, and evaluates many unlearning methods on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT across random and class-wise forgetting.
The proposed unlearning framework is simple and generic: it adds a conformal-prediction-inspired C&W-style penalty to existing training-based unlearning losses.
The paper provides extensive tables, multiple alpha settings, and appendix results, including a heuristic discussion of distribution shift for Random Label unlearning.
The Grad-CAM visualization in Table 1 gives an intuitive motivation for checking whether true labels remain in prediction sets, rather than only checking argmax predictions.
weaknesses: The central unlearning loss in Eq. 8 has a likely sign error. L_unlearn = max(S(x,y_t) - qbar, -Delta) is minimized when S(x,y_t) <= qbar - Delta. Since the prediction set includes labels with S <= qhat, this makes the true label more likely to be included in the conformal set, not excluded. The text after Eq. 8 explicitly states this encourages qbar - S >= Delta, which confirms the inversion. The loss should instead push S above the threshold, e.g., with a term like max(qbar - S, -Delta).

The CR metric is fundamentally problematic. CR = Coverage / Set Size. For forget data, a low CR can be produced by a large prediction set rather than true forgetting. In Table 4, FF has coverage 0.933 but set size 7.129, yielding CR = 0.131; the authors call this the best forgetting quality, yet the true label is still in the prediction set 93% of the time. This directly contradicts the stated goal of excluding ground-truth labels.

The treatment of UA is inconsistent. In standard unlearning evaluation, UA is accuracy on the forget set and lower is better, but the paper marks UA with an upward arrow and describes increases in UA as improvements (e.g., Table 7). This makes the empirical claims difficult to interpret and raises the possibility that the reported improvements are actually worse forgetting under standard definitions.

Conformal prediction relies on exchangeability between calibration and target data. The forget data after unlearning are not exchangeable with the clean calibration set, so the coverage guarantee and the threshold qhat are not valid for D_f. The paper acknowledges distribution shift only heuristically and does not establish validity for the proposed metrics.

The new metrics are not validated against an external ground truth or downstream privacy/security measure. There is no theoretical analysis of CR or MIACR, no comparison to existing uncertainty-based unlearning metrics such as Becker & Liebig (2022), and the 'limit-based' evaluation criterion is not formally specified.

The empirical evaluation has presentation and reliability problems. Several tables are corrupted or inconsistent, e.g., Table 11 contains coverage values greater than 1 (e.g., 1.189), impossible set sizes such as 10.000 and 200.000, and Table 14 has similarly broken entries. This undermines confidence in the reported numbers.

The 'gap to RT' criterion uses Retrain as a reference, but RT itself does not achieve ideal forgetting under the proposed metrics and is sensitive to hyperparameters. No statistical significance tests are provided despite only three trials per setting.

The proposed framework is applied to Retrain in Table 7, but Retrain is defined as retraining from scratch on retain data and should not use the forget data or an unlearning loss. This is conceptually confused and needs clarification.

The metrics depend strongly on alpha, calibration set size, and qhat. The paper recommends alpha=0.1 but gives no principled selection rule; when alpha=0.2, many methods produce set sizes below 1, leading to degenerate CR values and unstable comparisons.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is provided, the exact calibration split (whether calibration data come from the training set, test set, or a separate held-out set) is unclear, and the qbar update procedure, margin Delta=0.01, and lambda choices are not sufficiently justified.

The scope is narrow: only image classification on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet. The title's 'redefining machine unlearning' overstates the contribution, and the impact statement is generic rather than discussing limitations or potential misuse of the proposed metrics.

strengths: The core observation that a hard misclassification (UA/MIA 'forget' prediction) does not imply the true label is excluded from a conformal prediction set is a reasonable and potentially useful insight for the unlearning-evaluation literature, and it is supported by the mis-label/in-set counts in Table 3 and Appendix B.

The paper reasonably discusses two important design choices for conformal-prediction-based evaluation, namely calibration set size (Figure 1) and the choice of α (Section 2.3.2), and it honestly acknowledges a real weakness of the approach, i.e., distribution shift between calibration and forget data, proposing shadow/semi-shadow models to mitigate it (Appendix B.4).

The proposed unlearning loss is simple, implementable, and presented as a general add-on that can be combined with several existing training-based unlearning methods; the experiment table covers multiple methods (RT, FT, RL, GA, Teacher, FF, SSD, NegGrad+, Salun) and two datasets/architectures.
weaknesses: The conceptual foundation is shaky. Split conformal prediction provides coverage guarantees only for exchangeable (typically held-out) data, not for training/forget data. Because the threshold q̂ is calibrated on clean held-out data, coverage on forget data will be ≈ 1−α whenever forget data is roughly in-distribution, irrespective of how much the model has 'memorized'. The headline finding that ~54–90% of misclassified forget points remain in the set may therefore be largely an artifact of the calibration guarantee and of measuring distribution shift, not evidence of residual memorization. This directly undercuts the motivation for the entire paper.

The proposed CR metric (Coverage / Set Size) is ad hoc and unjustified. No theoretical grounding is given for why the ratio of two quantities that both depend on α and on the calibration distribution is a meaningful measure, and the stated interpretation is internally inconsistent (the same CR value is described as implying both successful unlearning and a utility drop). Empirically the metric behaves erratically: set sizes below 1 and as large as 10 or 200 appear (Tables 4, 5, 11, 14), and coverage is not comparable across methods when the non-conformity distributions differ.

The central claim that the proposed framework 'significantly improves forgetting quality' is evaluated almost exclusively with the paper's own new metric, and the loss L_unlearn = max(S(x,y_t) − q̄, −Δ) directly pushes the true label's non-conformity score above the very threshold q̄ used to compute CR. Improvements in CR are therefore expected by construction; the evaluation is circular/self-fulfilling. There is no independent evidence (e.g., retraining-based ground truth, gold-standard MIA, information-removal probes) that excluding the true label from the prediction set corresponds to genuine removal of information rather than a targeted adversarial manipulation of the forget label.

The claimed novelty is limited. Uncertainty/confidence-based unlearning evaluation already exists (e.g., Becker & Liebig, 2022, cited), and adapting the C&W margin loss to push labels out of prediction sets is a minor modification. The paper does not position itself adequately against this prior work or against other conformal/uncertainty approaches to unlearning, and the related-work discussion is thin and partly inaccurate.

Presentation and reproducibility are poor. Many tables are malformed or corrupted: Table 11 contains repeated/nonsensical rows and set sizes of 10.000; Table 14 contains spurious entries such as 'MAN-51, TAN-15' and set sizes of 200; Table 4 mixes metric rows into the method column; notation is inconsistent (q vs q̄, D_f vs P_f, D_test vs D_tcut); the λ grid is inconsistently reported as [0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.1] vs [0, 0.2, 0.5, 1]; columns referenced in the text (e.g., λ=1) are missing from the main table. These make it difficult to verify the reported numbers, and cross-references (Table 11 cited for both CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet) are wrong.

The empirical validation is narrow and weakly argued. Only image classification on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT is considered, only 3 trials are used, and the Grad-CAM argument (Table 1) is qualitative and does not establish a causal link between set exclusion and feature-level forgetting. The paper also does not demonstrate that any existing method fails on their metric for reasons other than the construction of the metric itself.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored gap in unlearning evaluation: misclassification under UA/MIA does not imply the true label is absent from a conformal prediction set. Table 3 provides a useful empirical demonstration that a substantial fraction of misclassified forget points (average 54.6% across settings) remain in the prediction set.

It proposes two evaluation metrics, CR and MIACR, and a general CP/C&W-inspired unlearning framework; the idea of using conformal prediction sets to assess forgetting is original and relevant to privacy and uncertainty quantification.

The empirical study is broad: 9 unlearning methods, CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, random and class-wise forgetting, multiple alpha and lambda values, and appendix ablations on calibration size and score distributions.
The framework often improves UA and reduces CR_Df while RA/TA and CR_Dtest remain relatively stable, and the non-conformity score distribution plots (Figs. 3-4) support the intended effect.
weaknesses: The central CR metric is unsound as a forgetting measure. CR = Coverage / Set Size can be low even when Coverage on forget data is high, if the prediction set is large or uncertain. For example, FF in Table 4 has Coverage_Df=0.933 and SetSize_Df=7.129, yielding CR=0.131, yet the true label is included 93.3% of the time. The paper calls this the 'highest forgetting quality,' which directly contradicts the premise that forgetting means excluding the true label. A trivial predictor outputting all classes would get CR around 0.1 and appear best, showing the metric is gameable.

The interpretation of Set Size is inconsistent and unclear: Section 2.3 says a smaller set size on Df implies the model cannot forget well, but CR rewards larger sets. No formal analysis explains how to trade off coverage and set size, and no coverage-conditional or set-size-normalized metric is proposed.

The conformal prediction step lacks theoretical justification for the forget set. CP coverage guarantees rely on exchangeability between calibration and target data; forget data are the target of removal and have a different score distribution. The paper only briefly acknowledges distribution shift in Appendix B, not for the main evaluation, and reports no theorem or guarantee for CR/MIACR.

MIACR is similarly heuristic. It counts only prediction sets exactly {0} and ignores {0,1}; a miscalibrated MIA classifier can produce high MIACR without genuine forgetting evidence. There is no validation that MIACR tracks true membership privacy better than MIA.

The proposed L_unlearn is a heuristic threshold loss without demonstration that minimizing it excludes true labels at the target coverage under distribution shift. The application to Retrain (RT) is questionable, since standard RT should not access or update on Df; the paper does not explain how the RT baseline and framework differ rigorously. Framework ablations report UA and CR but not the underlying coverage and set-size behavior, making it hard to verify the claimed improvement mechanism.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: several tables are garbled or contain implausible values (e.g., Table 11/14 with 10.000, 200.000, and labels like 'MAN-51, TAN-15'), method names and metrics are mixed in table cells (Tables 4, 5, 12, 13), and there are typos ('in addiction', 'CIFAT-10', 'Tabel', 'ReNet18') and inconsistent citation years. No code, hardware details, or exact calibration protocol are provided, and there is no limitations section.

The scope is limited to small image classification datasets and models; no larger-scale, non-vision, or certified-unlearning comparison is provided, so the claimed 'redefinition' of machine unlearning evaluation remains narrow.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting and plausible gap in existing unlearning evaluation: misclassified forget data may still remain recoverable through conformal prediction, which the authors term fake unlearning.

It proposes two conformal-prediction-inspired metrics (CR and MIACR) that go beyond point accuracy/MIA by considering coverage and prediction-set size, raising a useful discussion about reliable forgetting evaluation.

The CPU framework is conceptually simple and general: it adapts a C&W-style margin loss with a conformal threshold so that the true label is pushed outside the prediction set, and it can be added to existing training-based unlearning methods.

The empirical study covers multiple datasets, architectures, and nine unlearning baselines, with random and class-wise forgetting, multiple alpha/lambda settings, and visualizations (Grad-CAM, non-conformity distributions).
The paper includes a limitations section, discusses ethical/privacy implications, and provides a detailed appendix with additional results.
weaknesses: Central empirical claims are not reliably supported by the presented tables. Table 5/14 contain malformed and contradictory entries (duplicated CPU-FT columns, missing values, inconsistent names like CPC-RL, and values such as TA=50.97 at lambda=0.2 while the text says utility remains stable; CPU-FT lambda=0.5 UA=14.87 vs. RT UA=8.6, contradicting the claimed reduced gap to RT).

The CR metric can be misleading under distribution shift: when prediction sets become very large (e.g., RL on Tiny ImageNet with set size around 17.9), CR is driven toward zero by the denominator, and a low CR may reflect set-size explosion rather than genuine forgetting. The proposed shadow-model correction is not incorporated into the metric.

The use of split conformal prediction for forget-data evaluation is statistically problematic. SCP coverage guarantees require exchangeability between calibration and test points; unlearned forget data are deliberately made non-exchangeable with clean calibration data, so coverage/set-size guarantees do not directly apply, and fake-unlearning recovery ratios may not be valid diagnostics.

MIACR is under-specified and difficult to reproduce. It requires constructing conformal prediction sets over binary MIA labels, but the paper does not clearly define the calibration data, non-conformity score, threshold, or how membership labels are obtained for calibration in the unlearning setting.

The CPU objective is essentially an adversarial C&W attack loss. Pushing the true label out of the conformal set encourages confident misclassification/over-forgetting rather than explicitly removing data influence; no formal unlearning guarantee or privacy analysis is provided.

The optimization and evaluation criterion 'gap to RT' is ambiguous for UA. When UA exceeds RT (over-forgetting), the paper sometimes treats it as adequate, but over-forgetting should not be considered successful unlearning without stronger evidence of utility/behavioral equivalence.

Reproducibility is insufficient: calibration-set construction, separation of Dc/Dc-prime, model retraining details for baselines, hyperparameters, and code are missing or unclear. The malformed tables further hinder verification.
The reported improvement summary (average 6.6% UA improvement) is not traceable to the shown numbers; the average-gap calculations in the text conflict with Tables 5 and 14.

Baseline and metric comparisons are incomplete: the paper does not compare against recent uncertainty-based unlearning evaluation (e.g., Becker & Liebig 2022) beyond a brief mention, and statistical significance/variance analysis is limited.

Presentation quality is poor: many typographical errors (e.g., CIFAT-10), duplicated figure numbering, inconsistent notation (q-hat, q-bar, alpha, lambda), and table formatting make the core technical content unnecessarily hard to parse.
The scope is limited to image classification and two datasets; while this is acknowledged in limitations, the claimed general framework is not demonstrated on other domains or model families.

The method may create a mismatch between unlearning and adversarial robustness: intentionally maximizing non-conformity scores could harm calibration and reliability on retained/test data; Table 5 shows severe TA degradation in one setting, undermining the stable predictive performance claim.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: whether standard unlearning metrics such as UA and MIA actually certify forgetting. Using conformal prediction and uncertainty quantification as an evaluation lens is a creative direction.
It proposes concrete new metrics (CR and MIACR) and a plug-in unlearning loss (CPU), with experiments on CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, multiple baseline methods, and three trials.

The empirical observation that many misclassified forget points still have their true label in a conformal prediction set is provocative, and the Grad-CAM example in Figure 1 qualitatively illustrates the claimed fake-unlearning phenomenon.

The framework is simple and potentially general, and the limitations section and impact statement acknowledge some scope constraints, such as the focus on image classification and the need for calibration data.
weaknesses: The central conformal-prediction argument violates the exchangeability assumption. CP provides marginal coverage guarantees only for data exchangeable with the calibration set; forget data are targeted training data and are generally not exchangeable with the held-out calibration set. Therefore, coverage or set membership on Df cannot be interpreted as evidence that the model has retained or recovered the data. Under valid CP, roughly 1-alpha coverage should hold regardless of forgetting, so the reported high in-set ratios may be an artifact of applying CP outside its validity regime. This undermines the claimed fake-unlearning diagnosis and the proposed metrics.

The CR metric is theoretically and practically problematic. CR = Coverage / SetSize can be made low by producing large, uninformative prediction sets that still include the true label, e.g., RL on Tiny ImageNet has Coverage 0.969 yet Set Size 17.89 and CR 0.054. Set Size can also be less than 1, making CR > 1, e.g., NegGrad+ on Tiny ImageNet has CR 2.184, contradicting the intended interpretation. The metric conflates coverage and set size and is not a reliable measure of forgetting; it also rewards empty or near-empty prediction sets and is undefined when set size is zero.

MIACR is under-specified and not clearly valid. The paper does not provide sufficient details about how the MIA classifier is trained, calibrated, or converted into conformal prediction sets, nor how the nonconformity score for membership labels is computed. The rule C(x)={0} ignores empty prediction sets and can be satisfied by suppressing membership confidence, which does not establish that membership information has been removed. The reported MIACR values also depend strongly on alpha, which weakens its claimed stability.

The CPU framework does not demonstrate true information removal. Its loss is essentially a thresholded C&W-style confidence-suppression objective: it pushes the true label out of the conformal prediction set, but this can be achieved by reducing confidence or adversarial-style manipulation while the model still encodes the forget data. The paper does not evaluate stronger membership inference attacks, relearning attacks, canary insertion, influence functions, activation/parameter probing, or other privacy audits. Thus, the claim that CPU improves 'forgetting quality' or reliably removes influence is unsupported.

The experimental evidence contains serious inconsistencies and presentation problems. Table 5 is garbled, with duplicated method rows, 'CPC-RL' instead of CPU-RL, and implausible values such as TA 50.97 while the text claims stable utility, and CRDf 4.464 outside the expected CR range. Table 3 has confusing arrow directions and CR values greater than 1. The appendix class-wise tables are unreadable or contradictory. These issues make the main empirical claims difficult to verify.

The central empirical claim about fake unlearning is overgeneralized. Table 2 uses only RT, FT, and RL, yet the text claims 'in all settings, over 30% of mis-label data remains within the conformal prediction set.' Appendix Table 6 contradicts this for several methods, e.g., UA in-set ratios of 6.7% for GA, 10% for Teacher, and 8% for SSD. The reported 54.6% average is therefore selective and does not support the broad claim across existing unlearning methods.

Evaluation of the CPU framework is limited. Although nine baselines are evaluated under the metrics, CPU is applied only to RT, FT, and RL, while the abstract claims improvements for 'existing unlearning methods' more generally. The work is restricted to image classification, with no language or generative-model experiments. There is no formal theory, no code release, no statistical significance testing, and several hyperparameter/alpha choices are inconsistent or under-justified.

Reproducibility is weak. Important details are missing, including the exact MIA attack, shadow-model training, calibration splits, nonconformity scores for MIA, and how thresholds are updated during CPU training. The paper also contains multiple typographical and formatting errors such as 'CIFAT-10', 'addiction', inconsistent reference years, and duplicated/empty table entries, further reducing clarity and confidence in the reported results.

strengths: The paper offers a novel and timely framing of a limitation in machine-unlearning evaluation: existing UA and MIA metrics can label data as forgotten while conformal prediction still recovers the ground-truth label, which the authors call a fake unlearning issue. This is a useful diagnostic perspective.

The proposed metrics CR and MIACR are intuitive and directly motivated by the fake-unlearning problem. CR combines conformal coverage and set size, while MIACR gives a stricter conformal treatment of membership prediction. Both expose weaknesses of UA/MIA that are visible in the experimental results.

The CPU framework is simple and general in principle: it replaces the margin in a C&W-style loss with a conformal threshold and can be added as a plug-in term to existing training-based unlearning methods. The reported improvements on UA and CR while maintaining RA/TA are promising and computationally inexpensive.

The empirical evaluation is broad: CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, nine unlearning methods, random and class-wise forgetting, multiple alpha values, calibration-size analysis, Grad-CAM visualizations, nonconformity/softmax/loss distribution analyses, and shadow/semi-shadow handling of distribution shift.
The paper includes detailed training setups, hyperparameters, hardware, a limitations section, and an ethics/impact statement. Reproducibility is mostly supported at the experimental-protocol level.
weaknesses: The central conformal-prediction argument relies on exchangeability between calibration data and the target data being evaluated. Forget data after unlearning may not be exchangeable with held-out calibration data, especially in random forgetting where retraining can still generalize to forget samples. Thus, including the true label in a conformal set is not necessarily evidence of retained training information; it may reflect legitimate generalization. The main experiments do not fully resolve this, and the shadow/semi-shadow mitigation is only partial and largely relegated to the appendix.

The CR metric lacks a clear theoretical interpretation. Since it is a ratio of coverage to set size, it can exceed 1 (as seen in the tables, e.g., values above 2), is highly sensitive to alpha, and can be lowered by increasing set size even when coverage remains high. This makes the claimed monotonic relationship between lower CR and stronger unlearning questionable without further justification.

The MIACR metric is under-specified. It is unclear how the membership conformal predictor is calibrated, what nonconformity scores are used for MIA, whether the calibration data for MIA is independent, and how the binary prediction set {0} is constructed. These details are essential for interpreting and reproducing MIACR.

The CPU framework is claimed to be general, but the main text only applies it to a limited set of methods, mainly RT/FT/RL, while nine unlearning baselines are evaluated. The abstract's claim that it improves existing methods by an average of 6.6% is not clearly supported by the presented main-table numbers. Some table entries also show anomalous TA drops (e.g., TA 50.97 at lambda=0.2), which contradict the stated stability of retain/test performance and need clarification.

Presentation quality is notably weak for a top-tier submission: numerous typos and formatting issues (e.g., 'CIFAT-10', repeated or mislabeled rows such as CPU-FT/CPC-RL, duplicate figures, inconsistent alpha recommendations, misplaced or corrupted table entries), and several reference errors. These issues impede verification and reduce confidence in the empirical claims.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. While dataset/model/training details are provided, key aspects of the evaluation pipeline, especially MIA/MIACR calibration and the dynamic threshold update in the CPU loss, are not described sufficiently. The use of a negative constant in the hinge loss and the effect of updating the conformal threshold each epoch also deserve analysis.
